summary.name: Post Office Protocol
summary.one_liner: POP (Post Office Protocol), mainly POP3, is an internet standard application-layer protocol that email clients use to retrieve mail from a mail server.
use_cases: retrieving email in an email client
setting up POP3 access to a mail server
comparing POP3 and IMAP for email access
offline email access with temporary connections
understanding POP3 commands and session flow
summary.what_it_does: POP3 clients connect to a mail server, retrieve messages, and typically delete them from the server after downloading to the local computer. The protocol supports list, retrieve and delete operations, and a leave-on-server option where clients download only new messages identified by UIDL. POP3 listens on TCP port 110 unencrypted, with encryption via STLS or POP3S on port 995. The page also covers the history from RFC 918 (POP1) through RFC 1939 (current POP3), extensions, authentication methods like APOP and SASL, and a comparison with IMAP.
notable: Standard internet protocol defined in RFC 1939 with extensions via RFC 2449
Supports TLS encryption via STLS command or POP3S on port 995
Designed for download-and-delete use with temporary connections, unlike IMAP which keeps mail on the server
Includes a session example from RFC 1939 showing the command dialog
caveats: Original POP3 supports only unencrypted USER/PASS login unless TLS or an authentication extension is used
POP treats the mailbox as a single store with no folder concept and gives a static view of the mailbox during a session
POP4 is only an informal proposal with no progress since 2003
